summary: In this episode, Fathers Andrew Stephen Damick and Stephen De Young discuss the Orthodox Christian concept of theosis (deification/divinization) as the true understanding of salvation, contrasting it with Western Protestant and Roman Catholic views that focus on satisfying divine justice. They argue that theosis is not merely an individual moral improvement or a post-salvation add-on, but the very purpose of creation and humanity's destiny. The hosts trace the theme of becoming 'sons of God' and 'equal to the angels' from the promises to Abraham in Genesis (where his offspring are to be 'as the stars') through the New Testament, particularly in St. Paul's letters (Galatians 3-4, Romans 8). They emphasize that salvation involves adoption as sons of God, sharing in Christ's glory and authority, and participating in the divine council that governs creation. The episode also addresses listener questions on the role of demons in mental illness, the loss of this teaching in the West, and the difference between Protestant sanctification and Orthodox theosis.

concepts.title: Theosis (Deification/Divinization)
concepts.summary: The Orthodox Christian understanding of salvation as becoming partakers of the divine nature, becoming like God, and being adopted as sons of God, which is the purpose of creation and humanity's destiny.

concepts.title: Sons of God
concepts.summary: A term referring to angelic beings in the Old Testament, and in the New Testament, to humans who are adopted as sons of God through Christ, becoming equal to the angels and part of the divine council.

concepts.title: Promises to Abraham
concepts.summary: God's promises to Abraham that his offspring would be as the stars of heaven, indicating not just numerical multiplication but a qualitative transformation to become like the angelic beings who govern creation.

concepts.title: Divine Council
concepts.summary: The assembly of angelic beings (sons of God) who serve God and govern creation; humans are destined to join this council through theosis.

concepts.title: Sanctification vs. Theosis
concepts.summary: Contrast between the Protestant concept of sanctification as a post-salvation process of moral improvement and the Orthodox view that sanctification is theosis—becoming holy as becoming like God and joining the heavenly hosts.

claims.text: Theosis is not a metaphor or an adjunct to salvation; it is salvation itself, the purpose for which humanity was created.
Most Protestant and Catholic understandings of salvation focus on satisfying God's divine justice, whereas Orthodoxy focuses on transformation and union with God.
The promise that Abraham's offspring would be as the stars means they would become like the angelic beings who govern creation, not just numerous descendants.
St. Paul should be understood as a prophet and mystic, not a modern theologian, which affects how his writings on salvation are interpreted.
Sanctification, properly understood, is theosis: becoming holy means becoming like God and joining the heavenly hosts, not just moral improvement.
Mental illness and demonic possession are distinct phenomena, but spiritual influences can be involved in mental illness; they are not mutually exclusive.

Reiteration of the promise that offspring will be as the stars and all nations blessed.
God divided the nations according to the number of the sons of God, indicating the divine council.
Warning against worshiping the sun, moon, and stars, which God has allotted to all nations, equating them with divine beings.
Jesus says the sons of the resurrection are equal to the angels, connecting to theosis.
Paul says believers are sons of God through faith, baptized into Christ, and heirs according to the promise to Abraham.
Paul speaks of adoption as sons, receiving the Spirit, and being heirs through God.
Paul describes believers as sons of God, adopted, and fellow heirs with Christ.
Creation waits for the revealing of the sons of God, and believers await adoption and redemption of their bodies.
Paul says believers are predestined to be conformed to the image of Christ, so that He is the firstborn among many brothers.
